items.prose: A market data system stores each new symbol on one of 50 shards. Each symbol lands on a shard chosen at random, every shard equally likely, independently of the other symbols. A clash is two symbols on the same shard.

parts.question: Five new symbols arrive. What is the chance that no two of them share a shard? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: Each new symbol avoids the shards already taken: $\tfrac{49}{50} \cdot \tfrac{48}{50} \cdot \tfrac{47}{50} \cdot \tfrac{46}{50} \approx 0.8136$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the symbols one at a time; each must miss every shard already used.

byKey.your-shard: That is $\left(\tfrac{49}{50}\right)^4$, the chance no symbol joins the first one. Every pair can clash, so each new symbol must avoid every shard taken.
byKey.last-only: That is $\tfrac{46}{50}$, the last factor alone. Multiply all the factors, one per symbol.

explain.text: Symbol 2 avoids 1 used shard with chance $\tfrac{49}{50}$, symbol 3 avoids 2 with $\tfrac{48}{50}$, and so on. Independence lets us multiply: $\tfrac{49 \cdot 48 \cdot 47 \cdot 46}{50^4} \approx 0.8136$.

parts.question: Using $P(\text{no clash}) \approx 0.81360$ for five symbols, what is the chance of at least one clash? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. A clash is the complement of “no clash”.

byKey.none: That is the chance of no clash. Take it from 1.
byKey.from-your-shard: That is $1 - \left(\tfrac{49}{50}\right)^4$, a clash with the first symbol only. Any pair of the five can clash.
byKey.pairs: That is $\tfrac{10}{50}$, the 10 pairs times $\tfrac{1}{50}$. It counts runs with two clashes twice, so it is only an upper limit.

explain.text: “At least one clash” is the complement of “no clash”. So the chance is $1 - 0.81360 \approx 0.1864$.

parts.question: Using $0.81360$ for five symbols, add symbols one at a time. What is the smallest number of symbols for which a clash is more likely than not?

feedback.correct: Multiply on: 0.73224 at 6, 0.64437 at 7, 0.55416 at 8 and 0.46550 at 9. So 9 symbols pass one half.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply $0.81360$ by $\tfrac{45}{50}$, then $\tfrac{44}{50}$, and so on, and watch the clash chance.

byKey.half: That is half of 50 shards. A clash can happen between any pair, and pairs grow much faster than symbols.
byKey.union-bound: That solves $\tfrac{\binom{n}{2}}{50} \ge \tfrac{1}{2}$, the union bound. At 8 the true chance is 0.4458, still under one half.
byKey.root: That is about $\sqrt{50}$, a rough guide only. At 7 the chance is 0.3556.

explain.text: Multiply in $\tfrac{45}{50}, \tfrac{44}{50}, \tfrac{43}{50}, \tfrac{42}{50}$: no clash falls to 0.55416 at 8 symbols and 0.46550 at 9. So the clash chance first passes one half, at 0.5345, with 9 symbols.

parts.question: Using $n = 9$ symbols, what upper limit does the union bound give for the chance of a clash? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: There are $\binom{9}{2} = 36$ pairs, each clashing with chance $\tfrac{1}{50}$: at most $\tfrac{36}{50} = 0.72$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the pairs, then add a chance of $\tfrac{1}{50}$ for each.

byKey.one-symbol: That is $\tfrac{8}{50}$, the pairs of one symbol only. Each of the $\binom{9}{2}$ pairs can clash.
byKey.exact: That is the exact chance. The union bound adds the pair chances, which gives more.
byKey.ordered-pairs: You counted ordered pairs, $9 \times 8 = 72$. Each pair is one event, so there are 36.

explain.text: A clash is the union of 36 pair events, each with chance $\tfrac{1}{50}$. The union bound needs no independence and gives at most $\tfrac{36}{50} = 0.72$, well above the exact 0.5345.

items.prose: A lender tracks three borrowers, $A$, $B$ and $C$, each of which may be downgraded within the year. The risk team reports $P(A) = 0.10$, $P(B) = 0.08$ and $P(C) = 0.06$. For pairs it reports $P(A \cap B) = 0.03$, $P(A \cap C) = 0.02$ and $P(B \cap C) = 0.015$. The chance all three are downgraded, $t = P(A \cap B \cap C)$, is not reported.

parts.question: What is $P(A \cup B)$, the chance that $A$ or $B$ is downgraded? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the two chances, then take the overlap away once.

byKey.no-overlap: You added $P(A)$ and $P(B)$. The 0.03 where both are downgraded was counted twice.
byKey.both: That is $P(A \cap B)$, both downgraded. “Or” includes either one.

explain.text: Adding $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ counts $A \cap B$ twice. So $P(A \cup B) = 0.10 + 0.08 - 0.03 = 0.15$.

parts.question: Using $P(A \cup B) = 0.15$, write $P(A \cup B \cup C)$ in terms of $t$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Use $P(A \cup B) + P(C) - P((A \cup B) \cap C)$, and find the last term by the two-event rule.

byKey.minus-t: You took $t$ away. It is subtracted inside the bracket, so it comes back with a plus sign.
byKey.whole-overlap: You took $t$ as the whole of $(A \cup B) \cap C$. That event is $(A \cap C) \cup (B \cap C)$, with chance $0.035 - t$.
byKey.no-t: That leaves out the triple overlap. After the pairs are taken away, the outcomes in all three are not counted at all.

explain.text: $(A \cup B) \cap C$ is $(A \cap C) \cup (B \cap C)$, with chance $0.02 + 0.015 - t$. So $P(A \cup B \cup C) = 0.15 + 0.06 - 0.035 + t = 0.175 + t$, the three-event rule with $t$ added back.

parts.question: In $0.175 + t$, the value of $t = P(A \cap B \cap C)$ is unknown. What is the largest value $t$ can take? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: $A \cap B \cap C$ lies inside $B \cap C$, so by monotonicity $t \le 0.015$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The triple overlap is a subset of every pair overlap.

byKey.largest-pair: That is $P(A \cap B)$. The triple sits inside every pair, so it is capped by the smallest pair.
byKey.smallest-single: That is $P(C)$. The triple sits inside each pair too, and the pairs are smaller.
byKey.product: That is $0.10 \times 0.08 \times 0.06$, which assumes independence. Nothing says the downgrades are independent, and the question asks for the largest value.

explain.text: Monotonicity: $A \cap B \cap C \subseteq B \cap C$, so $t \le P(B \cap C) = 0.015$. With $t = 0.015$ every region of the Venn diagram still has a chance of 0 or more, so 0.015 can happen.

parts.question: Using $0.175 + t$ with the largest $t = 0.015$, what is the largest possible chance that at least one borrower is downgraded? Give a decimal.

feedback.correct: $0.175 + 0.015 = 0.19$, so the chance lies between 0.175 and 0.19.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Put the largest $t$ into $0.175 + t$.

byKey.singles: That is $0.10 + 0.08 + 0.06$, the union bound. The reported pairs pull the true chance below it.
byKey.smallest: That is the value at $t = 0$, the smallest possible. The largest comes with the largest $t$.
byKey.from-largest-pair: That is $0.175 + 0.03$, from taking $t$ up to the largest pair. The triple cannot exceed 0.015.

explain.text: The chance rises with $t$, so its largest value is $0.175 + 0.015 = 0.19$. With $t$ between 0 and 0.015, the chance of at least one downgrade lies between 0.175 and 0.19.

items.prose: Five cards are dealt from a standard 52-card deck, every one of the $\binom{52}{5} = 2{,}598{,}960$ hands equally likely. Let $A$ be “the hand holds at least one ace” and $K$ be “the hand holds at least one king”.

parts.question: How many hands hold no ace and no king?

feedback.correct: Take the 4 aces and 4 kings out: $\binom{44}{5} = 1{,}086{,}008$ hands.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Deal all 5 cards from the deck with every ace and king removed.

byKey.no-ace-only: That is $\binom{48}{5}$, which removes only the aces. Take the 4 kings out as well.
byKey.one-each: That is $\binom{50}{5}$, which removes one ace and one king. All 8 must go.

explain.text: A hand with no ace and no king takes all 5 cards from the other $52 - 8 = 44$. So there are $\binom{44}{5} = 1{,}086{,}008$ such hands.

parts.question: Using the 1,086,008 hands, what is $P(A \cup K)$, the chance of at least one ace or at least one king? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: The complement of $A \cup K$ is “no ace and no king”: $1 - 0.41786 = 0.58214$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. By De Morgan, “not ($A$ or $K$)” is “no ace and no king”.

byKey.none: That is the chance of no ace and no king. Take it from 1.
byKey.added: That is $P(A) + P(K)$, which counts hands with an ace and a king twice.

explain.text: By De Morgan, $(A \cup K)^c = A^c \cap K^c$, the hands with no ace and no king. So $P(A \cup K) = 1 - \tfrac{1{,}086{,}008}{2{,}598{,}960} \approx 0.5821$.

parts.question: One hand in about three holds an ace: $P(A) = P(K) = 1 - \tfrac{\binom{48}{5}}{\binom{52}{5}} \approx 0.341158$. Using $P(A \cup K) \approx 0.582137$, what is $P(A \cap K)$, the chance of at least one ace and at least one king? Give a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Rearrange inclusion and exclusion for $P(A \cap K)$.

byKey.product: That is $0.341158^2$, which treats $A$ and $K$ as independent. An ace in the hand leaves fewer places for a king.
byKey.once: That is $0.582137 - 0.341158$, with only one of the two singles. Inclusion and exclusion uses both.

explain.text: Inclusion and exclusion gives $P(A \cap K) = P(A) + P(K) - P(A \cup K)$. That is $0.341158 + 0.341158 - 0.582137 \approx 0.1002$.

parts.question: Using $P(A \cap K) \approx 0.100179$, how many of the 2,598,960 hands hold at least one ace and at least one king?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply the chance by the number of hands, then check with the counts.

byKey.union: That is the count of hands with an ace or a king. Both must be present.
byKey.from-product: That is about $0.341158^2 \times 2{,}598{,}960 \approx 302{,}490$, from treating $A$ and $K$ as independent.

items.prose: A short deck holds 20 cards: the ranks 10, J, Q, K and A in each of 4 suits. Four cards are dealt one at a time from the shuffled deck, and the hand is the set of 4 cards.

parts.question: What is the chance the second card has a different rank from the first? Give a fraction or a decimal.

feedback.correct: 19 cards are left, and 3 share the first card's rank: $\tfrac{16}{19}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. After the first card, how many cards are left, and how many have another rank?

byKey.replace: That is $\tfrac{16}{20}$, with the first card put back. It stays out, so 19 cards are left.
byKey.same: That is $\tfrac{3}{19}$, the chance the ranks match.

explain.text: After the first card, 19 cards remain and 3 of them share its rank. So the second card has a new rank with chance $\tfrac{16}{19} \approx 0.8421$.

parts.question: Using $\tfrac{16}{19}$ for the second card, what is the chance the first three cards have three different ranks? Give a fraction or a decimal.

feedback.correct: Two ranks are now taken, 8 cards, so 12 of the 18 left are new: $\tfrac{16}{19} \cdot \tfrac{12}{18} = \tfrac{32}{57}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The third card must avoid both ranks already dealt.

byKey.replace: That is $\tfrac{16}{20} \cdot \tfrac{12}{20}$, as if each card went back. The deck shrinks by one each deal.
byKey.fixed-bottom: That is $\tfrac{16}{19} \cdot \tfrac{12}{19}$, with 19 kept on the bottom. After two cards, 18 are left.

explain.text: As in the birthday problem, each new card must avoid every rank already taken. Two ranks hold 8 cards, so 12 of the 18 cards left are safe: $\tfrac{16}{19} \cdot \tfrac{12}{18} = \tfrac{32}{57} \approx 0.5614$.

parts.question: Using $\tfrac{32}{57}$ for three cards, what is the chance all four cards have different ranks? Give a fraction or a decimal to 4 places.

feedback.correct: Three ranks hold 12 cards, so 8 of the 17 left are safe: $\tfrac{32}{57} \cdot \tfrac{8}{17} = \tfrac{256}{969}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The fourth card must avoid three ranks, 12 cards.

byKey.replace: That is $\tfrac{16}{20} \cdot \tfrac{12}{20} \cdot \tfrac{8}{20}$, dealing with replacement. Each card stays out.
byKey.fixed-bottom: That is $\tfrac{16 \cdot 12 \cdot 8}{19^3}$, with 19 kept on the bottom. The deck has 17 left for the fourth card.

explain.text: With three ranks taken, 12 cards are ruled out, so 8 of the 17 cards left are safe. So the chance is $\tfrac{32}{57} \cdot \tfrac{8}{17} = \tfrac{256}{969} \approx 0.2642$.

parts.question: There are $\binom{20}{4} = 4845$ hands, all equally likely. Using $\tfrac{256}{969}$, how many hands have four different ranks?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply the 4845 hands by the chance.

byKey.suits-only: That is $4^4$, the suits for one set of four ranks. There are $\binom{5}{4} = 5$ sets of ranks.
byKey.ordered: That counts ordered deals, 1,280 times $4!$. A hand is the set of 4 cards.

explain.text: Every hand is equally likely, so the count is $4845 \times \tfrac{256}{969} = 1280$. In stages it is 5 ways to choose the four ranks times $4^4 = 256$ ways to choose their suits.

parts.question: Of the rest, 360 are two pair, 320 three of a kind and 5 four of a kind. All others are one pair. Using the 1,280 hands with four ranks, how many hands are one pair?

feedback.correct: $4845 - 1280 - 360 - 320 - 5 = 2880$, the commonest hand in the short deck.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The classes are disjoint and cover all 4845 hands.

byKey.at-least-pair: That is $4845 - 1280$, every hand with a repeated rank. Take off the other classes too.
byKey.no-quads: You left out the 5 four-of-a-kind hands. Every hand lies in exactly one class.
byKey.two-pair-ordered: You took 720 two-pair hands, counting the two pairs in order. The two pairs play the same role, so there are 360.

explain.text: The five classes are disjoint and cover every hand, so their counts add to 4845. One pair is $4845 - 1280 - 360 - 320 - 5 = 2880$, more than half of all hands.
